name: equal_effort_baseline_slowed
description: CALIBRATED AND RUN. The equal-effort question from the other direction: instead of speeding DeepSetsBotExp up until it evaluates as many positions per turn as the baseline, slow SakkirinaScaled down until it evaluates as few as DeepSetsBotExp. Same question, same target ratio, opposite side moved. SOT_BASELINE_TIME_SCALE=0.141 (= 1/r), timeout 12; achieved 6,433 vs 6,627 evaluations per turn over 400 games, matched within 3%. Read with equal_effort.json, which asks the same question from the other direction.
_why_two_directions: equal_effort.json and this config answer the same question by moving opposite sides.
Both were run because neither is decisive alone.
Speeding up the treatment (equal_effort.json) keeps the baseline at the timing its
author tuned it for, but gives DeepSetsBotExp an 88.2s per-turn budget, so the
measured agent is not the submitted one, and the run costs roughly 9x the wall clock
Slowing the baseline (this config) keeps DeepSetsBotExp at its competition timing and
costs a normal row, but runs SakkirinaSolo's search at about a seventh of the budget
it was designed for. Its rule-based fast paths and tree reuse do not scale with the
clock, so its play may change in shape, not just depth.
The two distortions differ in kind. If both directions move the win rate the same
way, the conclusion holds whichever side was moved. If they disagree, evaluations per
turn is not the right measure of effort for this matchup, and the equal-effort
framing needs revisiting before either number is reported.
This direction is cheaper and better matched (within 3%, against 0.88x), so it is
the one to lead with; the sped-up direction confirms it.
_calibration: Calibration, DeepSetsBotExp vs SakkirinaScaled, SOT_ALPHA0=0, both sides at scale 1.0:
n = 60 games, ratio of means r = 7.08 (roughly 6.4 to 7.8).
Both equal-effort configs derive from this one r, applied to opposite sides.
Achieved over the 400-game runs (quote these, not r):
DeepSetsBotExp 43,139 vs  SakkirinaScaled 49,131 evals/turn -- DeepSetsBotExp at
9.0 rather than r = 7.08 because evaluations per turn is only roughly linear in the
time budget (tree reuse and the rule-based fast paths do not scale with the clock).
A pilot at 7.08 undershot, and 9.0 was chosen from that pilot.
In both directions DeepSetsBotExp did slightly less work than the baseline (0.97x and
0.88x), so the residual mismatch works against the DeepSets agent.
_reproducing_this: To re-derive the scale on other hardware (the ratio is hardware-dependent):
prints r as a SUGGESTED SOT_TIME_SCALE. This config needs the reciprocal, since
2. timeout stays 12: both sides' bot-side cap is at most 9.8s (DeepSetsBotExp at
scale 1.0, the baseline below it), so the normal margin suffices. This is why
3. Re-run --calibrate with the filled-in values and compare the two evals/turn
figures. This direction matched within 3% at the first attempt.

matchups.label: equal_effort_baseline_slowed
matchups.note: DeepSetsBotExp is the fixed point here: SOT_TIME_SCALE=1.0 is exactly the timing it competes at, and SOT_ALPHA0=0 makes it the pure-network agent (behaviourally DeepSetsBot). Only the baseline's clock moves. SOT_BASELINE_TIME_SCALE=0.141 is 1/r from the 60-game calibration; it achieved 6,433 vs 6,627 evaluations per turn over the 400-game run.

matchups.label: calibrate_stock_speed
matchups.note: Identical to equal_effort.json's calibration block on purpose -- one measurement, both directions. Both sides at scale 1.0 measures the ratio at stock timing; the two configs then apply it to opposite sides. SakkirinaScaled rather than SakkirinaSolo because stock SakkirinaSolo emits no throughput telemetry, and at scale 1.0 the two are timing-identical.
